paras: The attempted lynching of the Corbett brothers took place in south Florida in the spring of 1888, when De Soto county stock owners seized the brothers at home on a charge of cattle theft and put ropes around their necks. After one brother was pulled off the ground, the stockmen gave them ten days to leave the country or hang.

According to a Globe-Democrat item, De Soto cattle owners had for months lost stock to 'a well-organized band of cow thieves' based in Lee county, nearly opposite Fort Myers. Informants in Myers said the Corbett brothers, called the gang's leaders, were selling cattle with 'bloody ears and poorly disguised brands' for the Key West market.

Before daybreak one morning, the principal stock owners surprised the Corbetts at home and demanded an explanation. The brothers took their guns and tried to ride off; one version says they were caught after a half hour's chase, the other that Winchesters brought them to bay after several shots.

With ropes around their necks, one brother was lifted off the ground over the limb of a water oak before 'calmer counsels prevailed.' The brothers reportedly confessed to selling hundreds of stolen cattle and promised to leave within ten days.

The coverage does not show whether the Corbetts left, and no arrest or legal action is reported. The item warned that it would 'go hard' with them if they stayed, since 'the cattlemen's word here is the only law that is respected.'

Only the stockmen's side reached print; no version names the brothers or gives a race. The People and Patriot of Concord, New Hampshire, ran a condensed version among crime briefs on April 19, counting four brothers. The full item, headed 'The Ropes Were Around Their Necks', appeared in the Lusk Herald of Wyoming on April 27 and the Phillipsburg Herald of Kansas on May 4. It treated the theft as established, calling it a 'nefarious business', and reported the near-hanging without criticism.
The brief counts four brothers and the fuller text three, and only the fuller text reports gunfire and a brother lifted off the ground.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of the Corbett brothers
bases: A body of De Soto county stockmen seized the Corbett brothers, put ropes around their necks and pulled one off the ground before relenting and ordering them to leave the country (A1, A3); it is an attempted lynching that ended in an expulsion order.

No one was killed: the stockmen relented after one brother was lifted off the ground and gave the brothers ten days to leave (A1, A3). The party acted without lawful authority on an accusation of cattle theft, but its size is not given (A3).

The brief in A1 is a condensed version of the same Globe-Democrat item printed in full in A2 and A3 (shared wording on the demand for an explanation, the seized guns and the ten-day alternative), so there is one account, from the stockmen's side.

accounts.label: Globe-Democrat item (stockmen's version)
accounts.gist: Stockmen informed by parties in Myers that the Corbetts were selling cattle with altered brands surprised them at home, fired on them, put ropes on three brothers and lifted one off the ground before pity prevailed; the brothers confessed and promised to leave in ten days.

accounts.label: Condensed brief
accounts.gist: Four Corbett brothers fled, were captured after a half-hour chase, confessed with ropes around their necks and were given ten days to leave or hang.

framing.detail: A New Hampshire weekly ran the episode as one item in a 'Criminal' news column, without comment or headline.

Western weeklies reprinted the Globe-Democrat item under 'The Ropes Were Around Their Necks', which treats the theft charge as fact and calls it a 'nefarious business' while noting that the cattlemen's word was 'the only law that is respected'.

conflicts.note: A1 is a condensation of the item printed in full in A3; the fuller text may be the better reading, but neither gives names.

versions.value: captured after a half hour's chase
brought to bay by the stockmen's Winchesters; several shots fired before they surrendered

conflicts.note: Not contradictory so much as differently condensed; only A3 reports shots and one brother lifted off the ground.

record_check.dossier: The stockmen were from De Soto county; the gang was said to be based in Lee county near Fort Myers; where the Corbett home stood is not stated.
No town is given for the seizure; Fort Myers, Myers and Punta Rassa appear only as where the cattle were sold.
Corbett brothers, four (A1) or three (A3); no first names.
A private party of stock owners with no officers mentioned and no lawful authority; not a posse.
Supported, with 'hanging' only partial: one brother was pulled off the ground and let down; shots were also fired (A3).
Cattle theft; the stockmen were 'determined to put a stop to this nefarious business'.
'Recently', before 1888-04-19; the month is not given and may be March or April.

the Corbett brothers, no first names or race given; four in A1, three in A3
accused of leading a gang of cattle thieves that changed marks and brands and sold cattle at Myers and Punta Rassa to buyers for the Key West market
